title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor A Circuit (Extended)
shortDescription: PCM detects an out-of-range signal on TPS A.
fullDescription: PCM detects an out-of-range signal on TPS A. The throttle position family demands a clean 5V reference and a smooth wiper; carbon, water intrusion, and a worn potentiometer cause most failures.
safetyImpact: Loss of pedal authority can engage limp mode without warning.

causes.cause: Worn TPS / APP sensor wiper
Carbon-fouled throttle bore sticking the plate
Damaged or chafed signal wire to PCM
Loss of 5V reference at the sensor
Throttle body actuator (DBW motor) failure
PCM internal driver fault

fixSteps.title: Scan and graph live data
fixSteps.instruction: Compare TPS / APP voltages at idle and WOT against the spec window. Sweep the pedal slowly and look for dropouts or signal flat spots.

fixSteps.title: Inspect the throttle body
fixSteps.instruction: Remove intake duct and check for carbon build-up around the plate. Clean only with throttle-body-safe solvent and a soft brush — never scrape the coating.

fixSteps.title: Verify reference and ground
fixSteps.instruction: Back-probe the connector. 5V reference and a clean ground must be present with the key on. Voltage drop on either side condemns the wiring.

fixSteps.title: Replace and relearn
fixSteps.instruction: After replacing TPS, APP, or the entire throttle body, perform the idle / throttle relearn procedure or the PCM may keep the code latched.

faq.q: Can I drive with this code?
faq.a: Short trips at light throttle are usually safe, but limp mode can engage suddenly. Resolve before highway driving.

faq.q: Will throttle-body cleaning fix it?
faq.a: Often yes if the plate is sticking, but a worn sensor wiper still needs the TPS or whole throttle body replaced.

title: Insufficient Coolant Temp for Closed-Loop (Extended)
shortDescription: Engine takes too long to reach the closed-loop fueling temperature.
fullDescription: Engine takes too long to reach the closed-loop fueling temperature. The coolant family is dominated by stuck-open thermostats; replace the thermostat with OEM-spec before chasing sensor faults.
safetyImpact: Long open-loop running raises emissions but does not cause sudden drivability loss.

causes.cause: Stuck-open thermostat
ECT sensor drift / out of calibration
Low coolant level / air pocket
Cooling fan running constantly
Faulty IAT vs ECT correlation due to harness short

symptoms: Cooling fan running at key-off briefly

fixSteps.title: Verify thermostat operation
fixSteps.instruction: After a 15-minute warm-up, the upper radiator hose should be hot and ECT should sit between 88-105°C. Cool hose with hot engine = stuck-open thermostat.

fixSteps.title: Compare ECT vs IAT cold
fixSteps.instruction: After an overnight soak both sensors must read within a couple of degrees. A divergence means one sensor has drifted.

fixSteps.title: Replace thermostat with OEM
fixSteps.instruction: Aftermarket thermostats often open early. Use OEM-spec part and a fresh gasket; bleed the cooling system per manufacturer procedure.

fixSteps.title: Check ECT sensor resistance
fixSteps.instruction: With the sensor unplugged and engine cold, resistance should be in the 2-3k ohm range. At 90°C it should drop to roughly 200-300 ohms.

faq.q: Can I just clear the code?
faq.a: It will return until the thermostat or sensor is corrected. The PCM rechecks warm-up time on every drive cycle.

faq.q: Does this hurt the engine?
faq.a: Long-term running cold dilutes oil and increases wear, but immediate damage is unlikely.

fixSteps.instruction: Remove intake duct and check for carbon build-up around the plate. Clean only with throttle-body-safe solvent and a soft brush — never scrape the coating.

fixSteps.title: Verify reference and ground
fixSteps.instruction: Back-probe the connector. 5V reference and a clean ground must be present with the key on. Voltage drop on either side condemns the wiring.

fixSteps.title: Replace and relearn
fixSteps.instruction: After replacing TPS, APP, or the entire throttle body, perform the idle / throttle relearn procedure or the PCM may keep the code latched.

faq.q: Can I drive with this code?
faq.a: Short trips at light throttle are usually safe, but limp mode can engage suddenly. Resolve before highway driving.

faq.q: Will throttle-body cleaning fix it?
faq.a: Often yes if the plate is sticking, but a worn sensor wiper still needs the TPS or whole throttle body replaced.

fullDescription: Pedal Sensor D and E voltages disagree by more than allowed. APP and TPS pairs are cross-checked: a single bad track will set both sides because the PCM loses correlation.

title: Engine Coolant Temp Sensor 2 Circuit High
shortDescription: Secondary coolant temp sensor signal stuck high.
fullDescription: Secondary coolant temp sensor signal stuck high. Many platforms add a head-side ECT sensor for spark and knock control; loss of either sensor disables compensation tables.
safetyImpact: Loss of secondary ECT increases knock risk on heavy load.

causes.cause: Stuck-open thermostat
ECT sensor drift / out of calibration
Low coolant level / air pocket
Cooling fan running constantly
Faulty IAT vs ECT correlation due to harness short

symptoms: Cooling fan running at key-off briefly

fixSteps.title: Verify thermostat operation
fixSteps.instruction: After a 15-minute warm-up, the upper radiator hose should be hot and ECT should sit between 88-105°C. Cool hose with hot engine = stuck-open thermostat.

fixSteps.title: Compare ECT vs IAT cold
fixSteps.instruction: After an overnight soak both sensors must read within a couple of degrees. A divergence means one sensor has drifted.

fixSteps.title: Replace thermostat with OEM
fixSteps.instruction: Aftermarket thermostats often open early. Use OEM-spec part and a fresh gasket; bleed the cooling system per manufacturer procedure.

fixSteps.title: Check ECT sensor resistance
fixSteps.instruction: With the sensor unplugged and engine cold, resistance should be in the 2-3k ohm range. At 90°C it should drop to roughly 200-300 ohms.

faq.q: Can I just clear the code?
faq.a: It will return until the thermostat or sensor is corrected. The PCM rechecks warm-up time on every drive cycle.

faq.q: Does this hurt the engine?
faq.a: Long-term running cold dilutes oil and increases wear, but immediate damage is unlikely.

title: NOx Sensor Circuit Bank 1 (Extended)
shortDescription: PCM cannot resolve the upstream NOx sensor signal on Bank 1.
fullDescription: PCM cannot resolve the upstream NOx sensor signal on Bank 1. NOx sensors are heated zirconia cells with their own ECUs; soot, sulfur, and bad DEF kill them quickly.
safetyImpact: Diesel emissions countdown will drop the vehicle to limp speed and eventually no-start.

causes.cause: Soot or sulfur poisoning of NOx sensor element
Faulty SCR catalyst / aged DEF dosing
Open or shorted CAN wire to NOx module
Incorrect DEF (water, low-quality urea)
NOx sensor heater driver fault

fixSteps.title: Read NOx live data
fixSteps.instruction: Capture upstream and downstream NOx ppm with engine warm at cruise. Healthy SCR shows >70% conversion across both sensors.

fixSteps.title: Inspect DEF quality
fixSteps.instruction: Use a DEF refractometer to confirm 32.5% urea. Cloudy or contaminated DEF will poison the catalyst quickly.

fixSteps.title: Check sensor heater
fixSteps.instruction: Heater current draw at cold start should pull about 2A then taper. No draw means open heater element — sensor is condemned.

fixSteps.title: Replace and code-program sensor
fixSteps.instruction: NOx sensors are matched parts; after replacement many platforms require coding to the module. Use OEM-spec scan tool functions.

faq.q: Why are NOx sensors so expensive?
faq.a: Each sensor contains a heated zirconia element and its own ECU. Aftermarket pricing usually starts at $250-$400.

faq.q: Can fuel additives help?
faq.a: No additive cleans a poisoned NOx sensor. Once contaminated, replacement is the only fix.
